6. I double-check my math and my logic. If I’m wrong, I own it. If I’m right, I show the proof.

8. If they ask why I did it this way, I say why—compliance, faster, less error, whatever. I back it up.

1. **Pause first.** Don’t say anything until I’ve finished. I’m not good at remembering who said what if I’m mid-sentence and someone else’s line’s getting cut off. It’s a habit, not a big deal.

2. **Look them in the eye.** Or at least pretend I’m looking. It’s easier to hear someone if they know I’m listening. Nod if it’s useful.

3. That’s it. I’ll say, “Wait, you said that part about the timeline—let me make sure I got it right.” Then I restate it back. If I got it wrong, I fix it. If I didn’t, I say, “Sorry, I thought you meant the delivery, not the packaging.” Simple.

4. Ask questions. “So you’re saying the client wants it by Friday, not Thursday?” That way I’m not guessing. If I’m wrong, I say so. If I’m right, we both know it.

5. Keep it clean. No “you’re wrong.” No “your method sucks.” Just facts, my method, your method. We both know it’s our methods, not us. We’re both trying to get this thing done right.

6. If we can’t agree, we split the difference or write down what each of us needs to check before we hand it in. Or we email it back and forth and argue over coffee. That’s fine. I like it when we actually finish the damn thing.

7. If it goes quiet, I say, “So next time we’ll both have the files updated by noon?” Or whatever. Make it a thing. Then we don next time.

If it gets ugly, I walk away. I’ve got better things to do than watch someone else fight over their own mess. But I’ll check in later if it’s still there.

Bottom line: I don’t care who’s right, as long as we both walk out knowing what we’re doing next. That’s the only win.

So, yeah. That’s how I do it.

Great question. Balancing availability for others and carving out time for deep work is something a lot of people juggle. It’s not about picking sides—it’s about making sure both get done, just at different times. Here’s how I’d think about it:

**1. Set the Rules Up Front.**  
Decide what “available” means and what “in the zone” looks like. If someone calls or texts, I check the clock. If it’s not one of my focus blocks, I say I’ll be right after this. That way, everyone knows when I’m switching gears.

**2. Schedule It.**  
Put meetings and quick chats in the morning or after lunch. That’s when I’m fresh and can still answer stuff. Save the real work for when the sun’s low and the noise is gone. Google Calendar’s color blocks help—blue for chit chat, green for work.

**3. Use a Two-Minute Rule.**  
If someone asks something that’ll take less than two minutes, I say yes. If it’s going to drag out, I say I’ll send a note. That keeps the little stuff done and the big stuff in my to-do list.

**4. Batch the interruptions.**  
If someone needs me for a thing, I grab a chair next to the door and wait till it’s over. Then I go back to my stack of problems that can’t be solved with someone else’s voice.

**5. Tell people when I’m full.**  
I put a sign up that says “do not ask, I’m in the middle of something.” If I’m not looking at my phone, I’m not thinking about replying. That’s the rule.

**6. Check emails at the top, not the middle.**  
First thing in the morning, I see what’s there. After that, it’s just noise. Same at the end of the day. If it’s not urgent, it goes back in the pile.

**7. Make the pile smaller.**  
I only keep three things on the desk. If it’s not one of those, it goes somewhere else. That way, I can actually finish the three before lunch.

**8. Say no to new stuff if I’m not done.**  
If I’m not done with my three, I don’t take more. That’s the only way I finish what I started.

**9. Plan for the next day after lunch.**  
I write down what I’ll do before I leave. That way, I know what’s coming and I can say yes or no ahead of time.

**10. Remember, it’s not a race.**  
Some days I answer more, some days I finish more. As long as I keep the schedule, it’s fine. The important thing is the work gets done and the people know when they can talk.

It’s not perfect, but it works. And if I get off track, I just start over. That’s the only way it gets done.
